title: ATLAS22kjn (AT 2022fpx): A Coronal Line Emitter with an Early Light Curve Bump and Mid-Infrared Dust Echo
comment: 34 pages, 18 figures, to be submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics (OJA). Comments welcome!
summary: We present an analysis of ATLAS22kjn (AT 2022fpx), whose high-ionisation coronal lines (CLs) and pre-peak light curve bump provide distinctive opportunities to investigate the physical mechanisms powering tidal disruption events (TDEs). In addition to CLs, the optical spectra show common TDE features, including a strong, blue continuum and broad Balmer and He II lines. The CLs appear before UV/optical light curve peak, preceding the detection of X-rays by $\sim 300$ days and persisting after X-rays are no longer detected, suggesting the X-ray emission is obscured at both early and late times. Using the CL luminosities, we constrain the temperature evolution of the ionising source, finding a decrease of $\lesssim 10 \%$ over 500 days. In the UV/optical light curve, we observe a $9 \substack{+4 \\ -2}$ day bump that peaks $125 \substack{+5 \\ -3}$ rest-frame days before the peak of the main flare. Although we cannot definitively determine the origins of the bump, we find that its timescale and luminosity are most consistent with theoretical predictions for a precursor feature produced by a stream-stream collision or a wind-stream collision. ATLAS22kjn also shows a prominent dust echo in its mid-infrared (MIR) light curves, indicating a high dust covering fraction $f_c \simeq 0.40 \pm 0.03$, similar to the covering fractions of other CL-emitting TDEs. From the multi-wavelength observations of ATLAS22kjn, we estimate the size and relative radii of the emission regions in its nuclear environment and determine that the CL region lies between the broad line region and the MIR-emitting dust. ATLAS22kjn demonstrates the importance of multi-wavelength and early-time observations, and the utility of CLEs in characterising the otherwise unobservable EUV/ultrasoft X-ray emission of TDEs.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes ATLAS22kjn (AT 2022fpx), a tidal disruption event (TDE) with high-ionisation coronal lines (CLs) and a pre-peak light curve bump. The CLs appear before the UV/optical peak, precede X-ray detection by ~300 days, and persist after X-rays disappear, suggesting obscured X-ray emission at early and late times. The study constrains the ionising source temperature evolution (decrease of <10% over 500 days), identifies a 9-day bump peaking 125 days before the main flare (consistent with stream-stream or wind-stream collision predictions), finds a prominent MIR dust echo with covering fraction fc≈0.40±0.03, and positions the CL region between the broad line region and MIR-emitting dust in the nuclear environment.
AI.motivation: To investigate the physical mechanisms powering tidal disruption events (TDEs) by leveraging the distinctive coronal lines and pre-peak light curve bump of ATLAS22kjn (AT 2022fpx), which provide unique diagnostic opportunities to probe otherwise unobservable EUV/ultrasoft X-ray emission and early-time phenomena.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength analysis of ATLAS22kjn including optical spectra (for coronal line identification and broad Balmer/He II lines), UV/optical light curve analysis (for the pre-peak bump), X-ray timing analysis (to correlate CLs with X-ray detection), coronal line luminosity-based temperature constraints, and mid-infrared light curve modeling to derive the dust covering fraction and emission region geometry.
AI.result: CLs appear before the UV/optical peak and ~300 days before X-ray detection, persisting after X-rays vanish—implying obscured X-ray emission. The ionising source temperature decreases by <10% over 500 days. A 9-day bump peaks 125 rest-frame days pre-flare, consistent with stream-stream or wind-stream collision predictions. MIR analysis yields dust covering fraction fc≈0.40±0.03. The CL region is located between the broad line region and MIR-emitting dust.
AI.conclusion: ATLAS22kjn demonstrates the critical importance of multi-wavelength and early-time observations for understanding TDEs, and highlights the utility of coronal line emission in characterising the otherwise unobservable EUV/ultrasoft X-ray emission of these events, while providing observational constraints on the physical mechanisms (stream-stream/wind-stream collisions) powering pre-peak bumps.

title: A Diverse Distribution of Black Hole Spins from Stable Mass Transfer
comment: Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!
summary: Gravitational wave observations have found over 300 merging binary black holes, yet their origins remain uncertain. Recent work showed that many may come from isolated stellar binaries whose orbits shrink through stable mass transfer. If true, their spins may help to distinguish this channel from other formation pathways. We investigate the tidal spin up of black hole progenitor stars with detailed modeling of binaries undergoing stable mass transfer. We calculate the tidal torques by solving tidally excited oscillation modes and predict the resulting black hole spins. We find a diverse spin distribution strongly affected by the mass transfer histories of the progenitors. Binaries can form black holes with moderate spins ($0.1\lesssimχ_\mathrm{eff}\lesssim0.3$) if they only go through case A or case B mass transfer. In the former case, they can become super-synchronized upon detachment, while in the latter case, the donor is usually only partially stripped, leaving a puffy envelope where strong tides are excited. If both case A and case AB mass transfer occur, the resulting black hole spins are almost always negligible. As the mass transfer history is jointly determined by mass ratio and initial binary period, our results predict an anti-correlation between black hole spins and mass ratio, consistent with limited evidence from data. Our results can also potentially explain the case of GW190412, a moderately-spinning binary with a high mass ratio. We discuss the limitations of our methods and additional physics (e.g., nonlinear tides, case C, and L2 mass transfer) that need to be incorporated in future work.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether tidal spin-up during stable mass transfer in isolated stellar binaries can explain the observed spins of merging binary black holes. Using detailed binary modeling with tidal oscillation mode calculations, the authors find a diverse spin distribution strongly shaped by mass transfer history, predicting an anti-correlation between black hole spins and mass ratio consistent with limited observational evidence, and potentially explaining GW190412.
AI.motivation: Over 300 merging binary black holes have been detected via gravitational waves, but their formation origins remain uncertain. Recent work suggests many may form from isolated stellar binaries whose orbits shrink via stable mass transfer. If correct, black hole spins could serve as a distinguishing observational diagnostic between this channel and alternative formation pathways. Understanding the expected spin distribution is therefore critical for interpreting gravitational wave observations.
AI.method: The authors perform detailed modeling of binaries undergoing stable mass transfer, focusing on tidal spin-up of black hole progenitor stars. Tidal torques are computed by solving tidally excited oscillation modes in the stellar structure, and the resulting black hole spins are predicted as a function of mass transfer history, which in turn depends on the initial mass ratio and binary period.
AI.result: The predicted spin distribution is diverse and strongly affected by mass transfer histories. Binaries undergoing only case A or case B mass transfer can form black holes with moderate effective spins (0.1 ≤ χ_eff ≤ 0.3): case A can lead to super-synchronization upon detachment, while case B leaves a partially stripped, puffy envelope where strong tides are excited. When both case A and case AB mass transfer occur, the resulting spins are almost always negligible. The results predict an anti-correlation between black hole spins and mass ratio, consistent with limited observational evidence, and can potentially explain GW190412's moderately-spinning, high-mass-ratio configuration.
AI.conclusion: Mass transfer history is a key determinant of black hole spins in the isolated binary formation channel, and spin observations can help constrain formation scenarios. The authors also identify limitations of their approach and call for future work incorporating nonlinear tides, case C mass transfer, and L2 mass transfer effects.

title: XRISM Spectroscopy of Variable Accretion-driven Disk Winds in NGC 4151: When, Where, and How Fast Outflows are Launched
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: X-ray observations probe the inner accretion flow within active galactic nuclei, revealing the highest gas column densities and fastest winds. The most diverse winds yet revealed with the Resolve calorimeter spectrometer aboard XRISM are found in NGC~4151, a nearby Seyfert-1 AGN that may qualify as a ``changing-look'' source (CLAGN). Herein, we report on wind variability in 14 XRISM observations of NGC~4151, summing to 0.9~Ms of exposure over a period of 395 days. We examined the dependence of key wind parameters on hardness and intensity selections, and as a function of time relative to flaring and dip events. The results suggest a globally organized but locally complex wind structure. Slow ``warm absorber'' components (WAs; $v_{\rm{out}} \sim 100-1000~\rm{km~s^{-1}}$) are always observed and likely represent failed winds at radius of $10^4 - 10^5 GM/c^2$, within the inner wall of the torus. In contrast, ``very fast'' and ``ultra-fast'' outflows (VFOs and UFOs; $v_{\rm{out}} \sim 10^3-10^4~\rm{km~s^{-1}}$, $v_{\rm{out}} \sim 0.033-0.33~c$) are strongest 10~ks after the peak of flares, and during periods with low flux. Ten kiloseconds is among the shortest flare--wind response timescales reported in an AGN, suggesting that the winds are observed close to the launching site. The absorption measure distribution (AMD) and the large outflow momentum rates suggest that the high-velocity flows visible in the Fe~K band are magnetically driven, while locally clumpy, likely owing to radiation pressure; one or both of these mechanisms may be enhanced following a flare and most visible during low-flux windows.

AI.tldr: This paper reports on wind variability in 14 XRISM observations of NGC 4151 (0.9 Ms exposure over 395 days). Slow warm absorbers (100–1000 km/s) are always present and represent failed winds within the torus inner wall, while very fast and ultra-fast outflows (10³–10⁴ km/s and 0.033–0.33c) are strongest ~10 ks after flare peaks and during low-flux periods. The 10 ks response timescale is among the shortest observed, suggesting winds are seen near their launching site. The AMD and outflow momentum rates indicate magnetically driven, locally clumpy high-velocity flows, possibly enhanced by radiation pressure following flares.
AI.motivation: To characterize the structure and variability of AGN outflows in NGC 4151 using a large, homogeneous XRISM dataset, and to understand the launching mechanisms and timescales connecting flares to wind responses.
AI.method: Analysis of 14 XRISM Resolve observations of NGC 4151 totaling 0.9 Ms over 395 days. Wind parameters were examined as functions of hardness, intensity, and time relative to flaring and dip events. Absorption measure distribution (AMD) and outflow momentum rates were used to probe driving mechanisms.
AI.result: A globally organized but locally complex wind structure was found. Warm absorbers (v_out ~100–1000 km/s) are persistent and consistent with failed winds at 10⁴–10⁵ GM/c² within the torus inner wall. VFOs and UFOs (10³–10⁴ km/s and 0.033–0.33c) peak ~10 ks after flares and during low flux. This 10 ks lag is among the shortest flare–wind response timescales reported. AMD and momentum rates favor magnetically driven, clumpy high-velocity flows in the Fe K band.
AI.conclusion: The winds in NGC 4151 are organized globally but clumpy locally; fast outflows respond rapidly (~10 ks) to flaring events, indicating proximity to the launch site. High-velocity Fe K outflows are likely magnetically driven with radiation-pressure-induced clumpiness, with both mechanisms possibly enhanced after flares and most visible during low-flux windows.

title: Long-duration GW Searches for Sub-solar NSs and Superkilonovae using CoCoA
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables
summary: On 2025 August 18, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration reported a sub-threshold gravitational-wave (GW) candidate, S250818k, consistent with a binary neutron star (NS) merger potentially involving a sub-solar-mass compact object. Follow-up electromagnetic (EM) observations identified a Type IIb supernova, SN 2025ulz within the broad localization area of the GW signal. This potential link between a sub-solar GW event candidate and a Type IIb SN, while not confirmed given the low statistical significance of S250818k, has nonetheless sparked renewed interest in the "superkilonova" scenario, where sub-solar-mass NSs form through processes like the fragmentation of an accretion disk or core fission in a collapsing star. In this picture, the in-spiral and merger of a sub-solar NS-NS binary is followed by the merger of the NS-NS remnant with the central black hole (BH), producing chirp-like GW signals. For sub-solar NSs with masses in the (0.1-1)M_sun range and BH masses in the so-called lower mass gap range of ~(3-5) M_sun, these signals can persist in the 20 - 1024 Hz frequency band of ground-based GW detectors for (10^2-10^3)s, potentially offering an opportunity to probe the superkilonova scenario, as well as the lower mass gap between NSs and stellar-mass BHs. However, the complexity of the underlying astrophysics may yield waveforms that deviate from standard templates, limiting the use of matched filtering in real GW searches. We therefore explore the detectability of such signals using the Cross-Correlation Algorithm (CoCoA), a more robust though less sensitive cross-correlation method. We discuss general strategies for implementing CoCoA superkilonova searches via either targeted follow-up of candidate chirps identified in matched-filter searches, or EM-triggered searches of stripped-envelope core-collapse SNe.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the detectability of gravitational-wave (GW) signals from "superkilonova" scenarios — sub-solar-mass NS-NS binary mergers followed by merger with a central black hole — using the Cross-Correlation Algorithm (CoCoA). The study is motivated by the potential link between the sub-threshold GW candidate S250818k and Type IIb supernova SN 2025ulz. The authors discuss that waveform complexity may limit matched filtering and propose CoCoA as a more robust alternative, outlining search strategies via targeted follow-up of matched-filter chirp candidates or EM-triggered searches of stripped-envelope core-collapse SNe.
AI.motivation: The reported sub-threshold GW candidate S250818k potentially linked to the Type IIb SN 2025ulz has reignited interest in the superkilonova scenario, where sub-solar-mass NSs form via accretion disk fragmentation or core fission. The authors aim to assess whether such exotic GW signals, which may deviate from standard templates, can be detected by ground-based GW detectors despite the limitations of matched filtering.
AI.method: The paper proposes using the Cross-Correlation Algorithm (CoCoA) — a robust but less sensitive cross-correlation method — to detect GW signals from sub-solar NS-NS binaries merging with lower-mass-gap BHs (3-5 M_sun). The authors discuss general implementation strategies for CoCoA-based superkilonova searches, including targeted follow-up of candidate chirps from matched-filter searches and EM-triggered searches of stripped-envelope core-collapse SNe. They consider signals in the 20-1024 Hz band lasting 10^2-10^3 seconds.
AI.result: The paper outlines how CoCoA can be applied to detect superkilonova GW signals that may evade standard matched-filter templates due to astrophysical complexity. It presents strategic frameworks for deploying CoCoA in both GW-triggered (targeted chirp follow-up) and EM-triggered (SN-triggered) search modes.
AI.conclusion: While not confirmed, the potential S250818k–SN 2025ulz association motivates renewed investigation of the superkilonova scenario. CoCoA offers a viable—though less sensitive—alternative pathway to search for these complex GW signals, potentially probing both sub-solar-mass NSs and the lower mass gap between NSs and stellar-mass BHs, provided robust search strategies are implemented.

title: From blue to red spirals: Slow galaxy transformation via ram pressure stripping in TNG-50
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Late-type galaxies lose gas through ram-pressure stripping (RPS) after falling into a massive halo. Because this mechanism primarily removes the gaseous component while leaving the stellar disk largely undisturbed, it provides a pathway for quenching star formation without immediate morphological transformation. While RPS is well established in galaxy clusters, galaxy evolution in low-mass groups is often attributed to mergers, leaving open the question of whether RPS alone can drive the transition from blue, star-forming spirals to quenched systems in these environments. We use the high-resolution cosmological simulation TNG-50 to investigate the evolution of blue spiral galaxies, after their infall into group-scale halos. We excluded systems undergoing significant mergers, thus isolating the effect of RPS. We find that RPS in low-mass groups (M$_{group}<10^{14.5}$ M$_{\odot}$) can efficiently quench star formation while preserving the stellar disk structure. The transformation is gradual, with quenching timescales $\gtrsim6$ Gyr after infall, longer than the $\sim4$ Gyr typically associated with merger-driven evolution. The resulting galaxies are predominantly red, anemic spirals rather than fully transformed S0 systems, indicating that gas removal alone is insufficient to produce complete morphological transformation. Our results show that RPS in group environments can generate long-lived quenched spirals which might represent an intermediate evolutionary pathway preceding the formation of lenticular galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using TNG-50 cosmological simulations, this study shows that ram-pressure stripping (RPS) in low-mass group halos can efficiently quench star formation in blue spiral galaxies while preserving their stellar disk morphology, producing red, anemic spirals over ~6 Gyr timescales—suggesting these represent an intermediate evolutionary pathway toward lenticular galaxies.
AI.motivation: While RPS is well established in galaxy clusters, its role in low-mass groups has been largely overlooked; galaxy evolution in groups is often attributed to mergers. The authors aim to determine whether RPS alone can drive the blue-to-quenched transition in group environments without merger involvement.
AI.method: The study uses the high-resolution cosmological simulation TNG-50 to trace the evolution of blue spiral galaxies after infall into group-scale halos. Systems undergoing significant mergers are excluded to isolate the pure effect of ram-pressure stripping on star formation quenching and morphological evolution.
AI.result: RPS in low-mass groups (M_group < 10^14.5 M_sun) efficiently quenches star formation while preserving stellar disk structure. Quenching timescales are ~6 Gyr after infall, longer than the ~4 Gyr typical of merger-driven evolution. The resulting galaxies are predominantly red, anemic spirals rather than fully transformed S0 systems.
AI.conclusion: Gas removal via RPS alone is insufficient to produce complete morphological transformation. RPS in group environments can generate long-lived quenched spirals, which may represent an intermediate evolutionary pathway preceding the formation of lenticular (S0) galaxies.

title: A Radiation-Hydrodynamic Light Curve Grid and Interpolation Framework for Stripped-Envelope Supernovae
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to AAS journal
summary: We present a grid of 8,148 stripped-envelope supernovae (SESNe) light curves based on radiation hydrodynamic simulations of exploding helium-star progenitors. The grid spans an ejecta-mass range representative of typical SESNe, together with broad ranges of explosion energies, radioactive nickel masses, and degrees of material mixing. We systematically investigate how these physical parameters shape the light curves and develop an interpolation-based parameter inference framework that enables the application of the model grid to observational data. Using the simulated light curves as mock observations, we assess the reliability of the widely used Arnett model. Although it reproduces the overall light-curve morphology, the inferred ejecta masses show no significant correlation with the true values. Moreover, the analytical model produces a spurious correlation between explosion energy and nickel mass, despite these parameters being independent in the underlying model grid. These results demonstrate that good light-curve fits do not necessarily imply reliable physical parameter estimates and highlight the need for physically motivated radiation hydrodynamic models in population studies of SESNe.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a grid of 8,148 simulated stripped-envelope supernova light curves from radiation hydrodynamic models, used to assess the reliability of the widely used Arnett analytical fitting model. The authors find that although Arnett fits reproduce light-curve morphology well, the inferred ejecta masses show no correlation with true values and spurious correlations emerge between explosion energy and nickel mass, demonstrating that good fits do not guarantee reliable physical parameter estimates.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate how physical parameters (ejecta mass, explosion energy, nickel mass, mixing) shape SESNe light curves and to critically assess whether the widely used analytical Arnett model can reliably recover these physical parameters from observational data.
AI.method: The authors generate a large grid of 8,148 SESNe light curves using radiation hydrodynamic simulations of exploding helium-star progenitors, spanning a wide parameter space. They develop an interpolation-based parameter inference framework and apply the widely used Arnett analytical model to the simulated light curves as mock observations.
AI.result: The Arnett model reproduces the overall light-curve morphology but fails to recover accurate physical parameters: inferred ejecta masses show no significant correlation with true values, and the model produces a spurious correlation between explosion energy and nickel mass despite these being independent in the underlying grid.
AI.conclusion: Good light-curve fits do not necessarily imply reliable physical parameter estimates, highlighting the critical need for physically motivated radiation hydrodynamic models in population studies of stripped-envelope supernovae.

title: Magnetic fields in extreme primordial halos: turbulent collapse and implications for early quasar formation
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: It is sometimes suggested that the most massive quasars at high redshift may have formed from rare high-sigma peaks in the cosmic density field. We explore here the evolution in a massive primordial halo corresponding to one of these rare sigma peaks, employing cosmological high-resolution magneto-hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations with initial field strength of $10^{-14}-10^{-8}$ G. The dark matter halo forms at the intersection of strongly convergent flows, leading to the formation of highly supersonic turbulence already on intergalactic scales, with turbulent Mach numbers of order $10-20$ also within the halo. Turbulent magnetic field amplification has never been explored in this regime and we therefore investigate whether this gives rise to effects similar to those observed in more typical halos. While the weaker initial field is somewhat more strongly amplified as a result of the shear flows, overall the evolution in the different simulations is rather similar and the flows are dominated by supersonic turbulence. We show in particular that the turbulent Jeans mass always dominates over the thermal and magnetic Jeans masses, and only on scales of $10^{-2}-10$ pc, the magnetic Jeans mass may become comparable to the thermal one. Our simulations thus strongly suggest the evolution to be dominated by the large-scale dynamics. As established in previous work, we thus expect the formation of central massive objects of a few times $10^4$ M$_\odot$ also in the presence of magnetic fields. The situation is somewhat different from more typical atomic cooling halos, where previous results have indicated a larger relevance of the magnetic Jeans mass on intermediate scales, potentially enhancing the mass of the massive object.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the evolution of massive primordial halos formed from rare high-sigma density peaks using cosmological magneto-hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations with initial magnetic field strengths of 10^-14 to 10^-8 G. The halos exhibit highly supersonic turbulence (Mach 10-20), and while weaker initial fields are more strongly amplified by shear flows, the overall evolution is dominated by large-scale supersonic turbulence rather than magnetic effects. The turbulent Jeans mass always dominates over thermal and magnetic Jeans masses, with magnetic Jeans mass only becoming comparable to thermal mass at 10^-2 to 10 pc scales. The authors expect formation of central massive objects of a few times 10^4 M_sun, though magnetic fields may play a more significant role in typical atomic cooling halos than in these extreme rare peak halos.
AI.motivation: Massive quasars at high redshift may originate from rare high-sigma density peaks. Since turbulent magnetic field amplification has never been explored in this extreme regime of highly supersonic turbulence (Mach 10-20), the authors investigate whether magnetic field amplification in these rare peak halos produces effects similar to those observed in more typical halos.
AI.method: Cosmological high-resolution magneto-hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations of a massive primordial halo corresponding to a rare high-sigma density peak, with initial magnetic field strengths ranging from 10^-14 to 10^-8 G.
AI.result: Weaker initial fields are somewhat more strongly amplified by shear flows, but overall evolution is similar across simulations with dominance of supersonic turbulence. The turbulent Jeans mass always dominates over thermal and magnetic Jeans masses; magnetic Jeans mass only becomes comparable to thermal mass on scales of 10^-2 to 10 pc.
AI.conclusion: The evolution in these rare high-sigma peak halos is dominated by large-scale supersonic dynamics rather than magnetic fields. The authors predict formation of central massive objects of a few times 10^4 M_sun even in the presence of magnetic fields. This differs from typical atomic cooling halos, where the magnetic Jeans mass may be more relevant on intermediate scales and could enhance the mass of massive objects.

title: Cherenkov light as a mechanism for light flashes seen by astronauts in space
comment: 44 pages, 22 figures
summary: Astronauts first reported light flashes during the Apollo 11 mission. These events have since been associated with cosmic rays, although their underlying mechanism remains uncertain. This study investigates possible formation processes using Geant4 simulations of cosmic ray interactions in a simplified model of the human eye. We apply published models of human visual perception to the simulated particle induced photons and compare the resulting light flash rates with experimental observations. Our results indicate that, in interplanetary space and in low Earth orbit outside the South Atlantic Anomaly, Cherenkov radiation generated in the eye produces retinal responses consistent with the observed frequency of astronaut light flashes. The dominant contributing primaries are found to be high Z nuclei, primarily iron, with additional contributions from oxygen and carbon nuclei. In contrast, conditions in the South Atlantic Anomaly suggest that additional mechanisms may be required to explain observed light flashes. We also find that the absence of light flashes at Earth's surface is consistent with insufficient retinal stimulation from muon induced Cherenkov radiation under typical geometrical and flux conditions.

AI.tldr: This study uses Geant4 simulations of cosmic ray interactions in a simplified human eye model to investigate the mechanism behind astronaut light flashes first observed during Apollo 11. The authors find that Cherenkov radiation in the eye from high-Z cosmic ray nuclei (primarily iron, with oxygen and carbon contributions) produces retinal responses matching observed light flash rates in interplanetary space and low Earth orbit outside the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA). However, conditions within the SAA may require additional mechanisms, and the absence of light flashes at Earth's surface is explained by insufficient muon-induced Cherenkov radiation under typical conditions.
AI.motivation: Astronaut light flashes have been observed since Apollo 11 and associated with cosmic rays, but the underlying formation mechanism has remained uncertain. This study aims to resolve this ambiguity by simulating cosmic ray interactions in the eye and comparing predicted retinal responses with experimental observations.
AI.method: The authors performed Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations of cosmic ray interactions in a simplified model of the human eye. They applied published models of human visual perception to convert simulated particle-induced photons into predicted light flash rates, then compared these predictions with actual astronaut observations across different environments (interplanetary space, low Earth orbit, SAA, and Earth's surface).
AI.result: Cherenkov radiation generated in the eye by high-Z cosmic ray nuclei—primarily iron, with additional contributions from oxygen and carbon—produces retinal responses consistent with observed light flash frequencies in interplanetary space and low Earth orbit outside the SAA. In the SAA, additional mechanisms may be needed. The absence of light flashes at Earth's surface is attributed to insufficient retinal stimulation from muon-induced Cherenkov radiation.
AI.conclusion: Cherenkov radiation from heavy cosmic ray nuclei is the dominant mechanism explaining astronaut light flashes in most space environments, though the SAA presents a case where alternative mechanisms may contribute. The study provides a quantitative framework linking cosmic ray interactions in the eye to observed visual phenomena.

title: Chemistry here and there: Comparison between the CMZ of the Milky Way and NGC 253
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, Proceedings of IAU Symposium 405
summary: For decades, chemical studies in external galaxies have been limited by sensitivity, resolution, bandwidth or a combination of them. A decade of ALMA operations, made the detailed study of the molecular abundances in nearby galaxies a routine job. We can finally bridge the ISM chemistry from Galactic to extragalactic environments, through one to one comparison, albeit probing significantly different scales. The ALMA large program ALCHEMI imaged the chemistry of the starburst galaxy NGC 253 at an unprecedented combination of sensitivity and resolution, achieving a detailed spatially resolved chemical inventory. ALCHEMI probed molecular differences among regions within its CMZ, and allowed the comparison with Galactic environments ranging from hot cores, quiescent molecular clouds and comets. This comparison can be put in the context of available data towards other extragalactic environments. Globally, the comparisons presented here show an astoundingly good correlation between the chemistry in Galactic GMCs and the central molecular zone of NGC 253, ranging scales from 1 pc up to ~0.5 kpc. The wideband sensitivity upgrade of ALMA will expand similar comparisons towards a wider range of Galactic and extragalactic objects.

AI.tldr: ALMA's ALCHEMI large program achieved unprecedented sensitivity and resolution in imaging the molecular chemistry of the starburst galaxy NGC 253, revealing a remarkable correlation between Galactic GMC chemistry and the central molecular zone of NGC 253 across scales from 1 pc to ~0.5 kpc.
AI.motivation: For decades, extragalactic chemical studies were limited by sensitivity, resolution, or bandwidth. The combination of a decade of ALMA operations and the ALCHEMI large program now allows detailed, spatially resolved molecular abundance studies in nearby galaxies, bridging ISM chemistry from Galactic to extragalactic environments through one-to-one comparisons.
AI.method: The ALMA large program ALCHEMI imaged the chemistry of the starburst galaxy NGC 253 with an unprecedented combination of sensitivity and resolution, producing a detailed spatially resolved chemical inventory. Molecular differences among regions within NGC 253's central molecular zone (CMZ) were probed and compared against Galactic environments including hot cores, quiescent molecular clouds, and comets, as well as other extragalactic data.
AI.result: The comparisons show an astoundingly good correlation between the chemistry in Galactic Giant Molecular Clouds (GMCs) and the central molecular zone of NGC 253, spanning scales from 1 pc up to ~0.5 kpc.
AI.conclusion: The wideband sensitivity upgrade of ALMA will enable similar chemistry comparisons to be expanded toward a wider range of Galactic and extragalactic objects, further bridging the two environments.

title: Radio flares and X-ray hardening embedded in the long soft state of 4U 1543-475
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present a comprehensive multi-wavelength study of the black hole X-ray binary 4U 1543-475 during its 2021 outburst, focusing on radio flaring episodes that are commonly interpreted as signatures of episodic jet production and are embedded within states when the X-ray emission was dominated by an accretion disk component. The radio monitoring reveals at least two discrete flares that coincide with periods of enhanced Comptonized X-ray emission. Broadband spectral modelling shows a significant decrease in the reflection-to-disk flux ratio (by a factor of ~3-4) during these episodes, consistent with a temporary change in the geometry of the inner accretion flow, although the data do not allow the causal sequence to be firmly established. Optical photometry exhibits variability that broadly tracks the reflection fraction, consistent with changes in the illuminating component. The accompanying spectral hardening indicates that the radio flares were associated with short-lived excursions toward a "harder" state, departing from the soft state. X-ray timing analysis suggests that the radio flares may be associated with changes in the fractional rms variability; however, no consistent or unified pattern can be firmly established across different events. These results provide a multi-wavelength observational example of radio flaring activity in a black hole binary and highlight the complex interplay between accretion flow geometry, coronal emission, and jet-related phenomena.

AI.tldr: A multi-wavelength study of the black hole X-ray binary 4U 1543-475 during its 2021 outburst reveals at least two discrete radio flares embedded in disk-dominated X-ray states, coinciding with enhanced Comptonized emission, a ~3-4 fold decrease in reflection-to-disk flux ratio, and spectral hardening—suggesting temporary excursions toward a harder state and complex interplay between accretion flow geometry, coronal emission, and jet activity.
AI.motivation: To provide a detailed multi-wavelength observational characterization of radio flaring episodes in a black hole X-ray binary during disk-dominated states, in order to better understand the connection between jet activity, accretion disk geometry, and coronal emission.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength monitoring combining radio observations, broadband spectral modeling (including reflection and Comptonization components), optical photometry, and X-ray timing (fractional rms variability) analyses during the 2021 outburst of 4U 1543-475.
AI.result: At least two discrete radio flares were detected coincident with enhanced Comptonized X-ray emission. The reflection-to-disk flux ratio decreased by a factor of ~3-4 during flares, optical variability tracked the reflection fraction, spectral hardening indicated short-lived excursions toward a harder state, and X-ray timing showed no consistent rms variability pattern across events.
AI.conclusion: The radio flaring activity in this soft-state outburst is associated with temporary geometric changes in the inner accretion flow and spectral hardening, but the causal ordering and a unified timing signature could not be firmly established, highlighting the complex coupling between jets, coronae, and accretion disk structure.

title: Testing Covarying Coupling Constants (CCC) against the full SPARC rotation-curve sample: a like-for-like comparison with MOND and NFW
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables, a montage of 165 galaxy rotation curves as supplementary material. Comments are welcomed
summary: The Covarying Coupling Constants (CCC) framework, developed to account for high-redshift JWST observations, contains a mechanism -- a covarying-constant effective mass field keyed to local density -- that modifies galactic dynamics without particle dark matter. We test it against the full Spitzer Photometry and Accurate Rotation Curves (SPARC) sample of 175 disc galaxies, extending an earlier study of a few objects. Working in an inverse formulation, in which each model predicts the baryonic rotation curve from the observed one, we compare CCC against Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and one- and two-parameter Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) haloes on identical footing, using the reduced $χ^2_ν$. We show that the published sharp density turn-off in the earlier study is unphysical and replace it with a smooth transition -- the density-space analogue of the MOND interpolating function, introducing no new parameter. One-parameter smooth-CCC then performs comparably to galaxy-by-galaxy fitted MOND (the lower $χ^2_ν$ in 56 per cent of galaxies, mean $χ^2_ν$ of 2.58 versus 2.65; the paired difference is not significant), while two-parameter NFW shows a substantially broader fit-quality distribution and a larger tail of poor or boundary-limited fits (mean $χ^2_ν\approx 7$). The CCC turn-off density is not universal (scatter 0.82 dex) and correlates with galaxy size, qualitatively consistent with a spherical reconstruction applied to flattened disc systems. Recast as an acceleration, however, $a_t = V_{\rm flat}^2/R_t$ has scatter 0.33 dex (on the 91-galaxy resolved subset) -- matching the MOND scale $a_0$ (0.34 dex) -- and comparable magnitude of order $2 \times 10^{-10}$ m/s$^2$, with its size correlation removed. Though not designed for galactic dynamics, CCC describes rotation curves as well as galaxy-by-galaxy fitted MOND.

The authors replace an unphysical sharp density turn-off with a smooth transition (analogous to MOND's interpolating function) with no extra parameters. One-parameter smooth-CCC performs comparably to galaxy-by-galaxy fitted MOND, while two-parameter NFW shows substantially worse and broader fit-quality distributions. The CCC turn-off density is non-universal and correlates with galaxy size, but when recast as an acceleration it matches the MOND scale a0 in both scatter and magnitude, removing the size correlation.
AI.motivation: To test whether the CCC framework, originally developed to explain high-redshift JWST observations, can also account for galactic dynamics in nearby disc galaxies without invoking particle dark matter, extending an earlier small-sample study to the full SPARC dataset on equal footing with MOND and NFW models.
AI.method: Using an inverse formulation where each model predicts the baryonic rotation curve from the observed one, the authors compare one-parameter smooth-CCC (with a smooth density transition replacing the unphysical sharp turn-off) against galaxy-by-galaxy fitted MOND and one- and two-parameter NFW haloes, quantified via reduced chi-squared (χ²_ν). Statistical comparisons are made using paired differences and distribution analysis.
AI.result: Smooth-CCC performs comparably to MOND: lower χ²_ν in 56% of galaxies with mean χ²_ν of 2.58 versus 2.65, a non-significant paired difference. Two-parameter NFW shows a substantially broader fit-quality distribution with larger tails of poor or boundary-limited fits (mean χ²_ν ≈ 7). The CCC turn-off density has 0.82 dex scatter and correlates with galaxy size; recast as an acceleration a_t, the scatter drops to 0.33 dex (matching MOND's a0 at 0.34 dex), with magnitude ~2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s² and the size correlation removed.
AI.conclusion: Though not designed for galactic dynamics, the CCC framework describes rotation curves as well as galaxy-by-galaxy fitted MOND, and its key scale matches the MOND acceleration a0. The size correlation of the turn-off density is consistent with a spherical reconstruction applied to flattened discs, suggesting the apparent non-universality is a geometric artifact rather than a physical failure.

title: Discovery of 27 new Rotating Radio Transients by MeerTRAP
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
summary: We present the discovery of 27 new Galactic transients made by the commensal MeerTRAP single pulse search programme at the MeerKAT telescope. We determine the location of 14 of these discoveries with arcsecond accuracy by imaging the data captured in the dedicated transient buffer. A preliminary estimate of the period was made for 8 sources using the arrival times of several pulses detected by MeerTRAP. The periods of these transients range between 0.78 s and 4 s. For the previously published MeerTRAP source MTP0040 (PSR J1357-6507), we are able to provide the position and period using new pulses detected since it was reported. We also estimate the radio fluences and discuss the burst rates derived from the commensal search detections. The accurate image-domain localizations were used to conduct follow-up observations and timing analysis. Furthermore, some follow-up observations revealed ordinary pulsar-like pulsed behavior for four of the new sources, illustrating the blurred separation between rotating radio transients and canonical pulsars. We also present coherent timing solutions for 4 sources, providing insight into their rotational properties and their place within the Galactic neutron star population.

AI.tldr: The MeerTRAP programme at the MeerKAT telescope discovered 27 new Galactic radio transients, of which 14 were localized with arcsecond accuracy via imaging, 8 had preliminary periods estimated (0.78–4 s), and follow-up observations revealed pulsar-like behavior for 4 sources with coherent timing solutions.
AI.motivation: To discover and characterize new Galactic radio transients (likely rotating radio transients and pulsars) to better understand the neutron star population and the blurred distinction between transient and canonical pulsar behavior.
AI.method: Commensal MeerTRAP single pulse search programme at MeerKAT; imaging of transient buffer data for arcsecond-level localization; arrival time analysis for period estimation; follow-up observations and coherent timing analysis for selected sources.
AI.result: 27 new Galactic transients discovered; 14 localized to arcsecond accuracy; periods estimated for 8 sources ranging 0.78–4 s; position and period refinement for MTP0040; radio fluences and burst rates reported; 4 sources showed ordinary pulsar-like pulsed behavior in follow-up; coherent timing solutions obtained for 4 sources.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the success of commensal searching for radio transients, reveal that many RRATs are likely canonical pulsars with intermittent emission, and provide timing solutions that place the new sources within the Galactic neutron star population.

title: Molecule-specific diffusion and desorption of interstellar ices on carbonaceous dust
summary: Interstellar ices form on dust grains in the coldest regions of molecular clouds and preserve key volatile reservoirs that could be incorporated into protoplanetary disks during star and planet formation. However, the effect of the dust surface composition on the ice structure and spectroscopic behavior remains poorly constrained. We present a comparative laboratory study of astrophysically relevant ices (CO, CO2, and H2O) deposited on inert calcium fluoride (CaF2) substrate and carbonaceous dust analogs under interstellar conditions. Infrared spectroscopy and temperature-programmed desorption reveal pronounced molecule-specific infrared spectral responses to the amorphous carbonaceous surface. CO and CO2 both exhibit broadened absorption bands, redshifted band positions, and delayed desorption, arising from thermally activated diffusion into the porous dust matrix and indicating strong molecule-surface interactions. By contrast, H2O varies only very little spectrally and thermally, indicating weak wetting and limited coupling to the substrate. These results provide direct laboratory evidence that dust-ice interfaces can affect the ice structure and desorption kinetics of interstellar ices even in thick ice layers. These findings offer new constraints for interpreting infrared absorption bands in astronomical observations and highlight the importance of surface effects in models of interstellar ice chemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a laboratory study comparing interstellar ice analogs (CO, CO2, H2O) deposited on inert CaF2 substrates versus carbonaceous dust analogs, revealing that carbonaceous surfaces induce molecule-specific spectral broadening, redshifted absorption bands, and delayed desorption for CO and CO2 due to diffusion into the porous dust matrix, while H2O remains largely unaffected.
AI.motivation: The effect of dust surface composition on ice structure and spectroscopic behavior is poorly constrained, yet critical for interpreting astronomical observations and understanding volatile reservoirs in molecular clouds and protoplanetary disks.
AI.method: Comparative laboratory experiments depositing astrophysically relevant ices (CO, CO2, H2O) on inert CaF2 substrates and amorphous carbonaceous dust analogs under interstellar conditions, characterized using infrared spectroscopy and temperature-programmed desorption.
AI.result: CO and CO2 show broadened absorption bands, redshifted band positions, and delayed desorption on carbonaceous surfaces due to thermally activated diffusion into the porous dust matrix and strong molecule-surface interactions, whereas H2O exhibits minimal spectral and thermal variations, indicating weak wetting and limited substrate coupling.
AI.conclusion: Dust-ice interfaces can affect ice structure and desorption kinetics even in thick ice layers, providing new constraints for interpreting infrared absorption bands in astronomical observations and highlighting the importance of surface effects in interstellar ice chemistry models.

title: Spiral structure from the interference of gravitational eigenmodes in ultralight dark matter halos
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures
summary: We use a variety of analytic and numerical techniques to approximate the geometry of individual dark matter halos when modeled as collections of ultralight scalar bosons (ULDM), followed by an analysis on the future directions and implications of this work. Ultimately, we aim to understand the morphology and creation of complex structures (like spirals) in galaxies from a geometric standpoint and to investigate the connection between dark matter and baryonic matter in galaxies. We find that superpositions of gravitational eigenmodes for ULDM in a fixed background potential can yield spiral density perturbations which rotate on the order of one hundred million years and appear within ten to twenty kpc of the halo center, both features comparable to realistic galaxies, and that this model provides a natural explanation for the density waves necessary to seed baryonic spirals.

AI.tldr: The paper models dark matter halos as collections of ultralight scalar bosons (ULDM) and uses analytic and numerical techniques to approximate their geometry. Superpositions of gravitational eigenmodes in a fixed background potential produce spiral density perturbations that rotate on ~100 million year timescales and appear within 10-20 kpc of the halo center—features comparable to real galaxies—providing a natural seeding mechanism for baryonic spiral density waves.
AI.motivation: To understand the morphology and creation of complex structures (like spirals) in galaxies from a geometric standpoint and to investigate the connection between dark matter and baryonic matter in galaxies.
AI.method: A combination of analytic and numerical techniques to approximate the geometry of individual dark matter halos modeled as collections of ultralight scalar bosons (ULDM), by examining superpositions of gravitational eigenmodes in a fixed background potential.
AI.result: Superpositions of ULDM gravitational eigenmodes yield spiral density perturbations that rotate on ~100 million year timescales and appear within 10-20 kpc of the halo center, both comparable to realistic galaxies.
AI.conclusion: This ULDM model provides a natural explanation for the density waves necessary to seed baryonic spirals, linking dark matter halo geometry to observable galactic structure.

title: Classifying Quasar Types Without a Spectrum
comment: 22 pages, 15 figures. Accepted for publication in PASP
summary: Distinguishing between Type 1 and Type 2 quasars is important because it helps us understand accretion regimes, black hole mass scaling, disk instabilities and feedback processes in active galaxies. Although spectroscopy provides robust classification, it does not scale well with the millions of quasars observed in modern surveys, as it requires substantial time and resources to acquire a good spectrum. On the photometry side, quasar light curves are always irregularly sampled and affected by the specifics of photometric surveys, making them difficult to analyze. In this work, we show that we can use irregularly sampled light curves from the Zwicky Transient Facility to classify quasar types without a spectrum, using Slepian Wavelet Variance. This technique allows us to decompose the variance of light curves into multiple timescales. We use agglomerative hierarchical clustering to classify 516 Type 1 and 238 Type 2 quasars from the MILLIQUAS catalogue, solely based on their wavelet variance curves. We obtain a recovery rate of 99% for Type 1 and 87% for Type 2 quasars, and the few misclassified quasars show the opposite variability behaviour to their spectral type. In contrast to structure functions and the Damped Random Walk model, Slepian Wavelet Variance offers a complementary, model-independent view of variability across short and long timescales.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates that quasar types (Type 1 vs Type 2) can be classified without spectroscopy using irregularly sampled Zwicky Transient Facility light curves via Slepian Wavelet Variance, achieving 99% recovery for Type 1 and 87% for Type 2 quasars through agglomerative hierarchical clustering on variance curves decomposed across multiple timescales.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing Type 1 and Type 2 quasars is important for understanding accretion regimes, black hole mass scaling, disk instabilities, and feedback processes. While spectroscopy offers robust classification, it does not scale to the millions of quasars in modern surveys. Photometric light curves are irregularly sampled and survey-dependent, making them difficult to analyze with existing methods.
AI.method: The authors apply Slepian Wavelet Variance to decompose the variance of irregularly sampled Zwicky Transient Facility light curves into multiple timescales. They then use agglomerative hierarchical clustering to classify 516 Type 1 and 238 Type 2 quasars from the MILLIQUAS catalogue based solely on their wavelet variance curves.

The approach is model-independent and complementary to structure functions and the Damped Random Walk model, covering both short and long timescales.
AI.conclusion: Slepian Wavelet Variance provides an effective, scalable, and model-independent photometric alternative to spectroscopy for quasar type classification, overcoming the challenges of irregular sampling in real survey data.

title: Identification of a Large-Scale Diffuse Gamma-Ray Structure in the Southern Galactic Hemisphere
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, accepted by ApJ
summary: We identify and characterize a large-scale diffuse gamma-ray structure in the Southern Galactic Hemisphere using 17 yr of Fermi-LAT data. An energy-dependent likelihood analysis, including alternative Galactic diffuse-emission models, isotropic emission, the Fermi bubbles, and resolved 4FGL sources, reveals an extended excess that persists across the tested background models and spans tens of degrees. The excess broadly follows the X-ray-defined southern eROSITA Bubble (eB) region, while also overlapping the projected southern extension of Loop I. Template fits favor a filled eB-like morphology over the adopted Wolleben Loop I shell geometry, making the structure a plausible gamma-ray counterpart of the southern eB, although Loop-I-related or other localized foreground emission cannot be excluded. Under the eB template, the southern component is fainter and softer than the northern large-scale component, with an integrated luminosity lower by a factor of about seven, broadly consistent with the eROSITA-bubble asymmetry. If interpreted as Galactic-scale outflow emission, its faint, soft spectrum may indicate aged particles and/or distributed reacceleration in the outer bubble. A hadronic interpretation is energetically demanding, whereas a leptonic inverse-Compton scenario is more economical but requires rapid transport and/or local reacceleration of high-energy electrons.

The excess is fainter and softer than the northern counterpart, with an integrated luminosity lower by a factor of ~7, suggesting aged particles or distributed reacceleration if interpreted as Galactic outflow emission.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize the gamma-ray counterpart of the southern eROSITA Bubble and understand its physical origin, particularly whether Galactic-scale outflow emission extends to the southern hemisphere with properties consistent with the asymmetric eROSITA bubbles.
AI.method: Energy-dependent likelihood analysis of 17 years of Fermi-LAT data, incorporating alternative Galactic diffuse-emission models, isotropic emission, Fermi bubbles, and resolved 4FGL sources. The excess was tested against multiple background models and fitted with morphological templates comparing a filled eB-like morphology versus the Wolleben Loop I shell geometry.

Template fits favor a filled eB-like morphology. The southern component is fainter and softer than the northern counterpart, with integrated luminosity lower by ~7x, consistent with eB asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: The structure is a plausible gamma-ray counterpart of the southern eB. If interpreted as Galactic outflow emission, its faint soft spectrum suggests aged particles and/or distributed reacceleration in the outer bubble. title: Search for a Globular Cluster whose Passage through the Galactic Disk could Trigger the Radcliffe Wave
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Astrophysical Bulletin
summary: Using a catalog of 152 globular clusters (GCs), their orbits were constructed to determine their intersections with the Galaxy's plane of symmetry. Young open star clusters (OSCs) were selected from the selection zone characteristic of the Radcliffe wave. The Hunt and Reffert catalog served as the source of data on these OSCs. A grouping of 17 OSCs with an average age of 32.7 million years was found. It is compact in coordinate, velocity, and age space. This grouping is shown to be a good candidate for the hypothesis that the Radcliffe wave is generated by the passage of an impactor through the Galaxy's plane of symmetry, with the impactor being the GC NGC~4372. The last time it crossed the galactic plane was 55.5 million years ago, and 22.2 million years later, a burst of star formation occurred at this location, forming a whole group of open-clustered stars, and possibly the Radcliffe wave as a whole.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that the globular cluster NGC 4372, which crossed the Galactic plane 55.5 Myr ago, triggered a star formation burst 22.2 Myr later that produced a compact group of 17 young open clusters (average age 32.7 Myr) associated with the Radcliffe wave.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that the Radcliffe wave—a large-scale coherent star-forming structure in the Milky Way—was generated by the passage of an impacting body (a globular cluster) through the Galactic plane.
AI.method: Orbits of 152 globular clusters were computed to find their intersections with the Galactic plane. Young open star clusters were selected from the Radcliffe wave characteristic selection zone using the Hunt and Reffert catalog, and their positions, velocities, and ages were analyzed.
AI.result: A compact grouping of 17 open star clusters with an average age of 32.7 Myr was identified. The globular cluster NGC 4372 crossed the Galactic plane 55.5 Myr ago; 22.2 Myr later, a star formation burst occurred at that location, forming the open cluster group and possibly the Radcliffe wave.
AI.conclusion: The identified grouping is a strong candidate supporting the hypothesis that NGC 4372's passage through the Galactic plane seeded the star formation burst that gave rise to the Radcliffe wave.

title: Constraining the gamma-ray efficiency of LINER outflows with Fermi-LAT and MEGARA
comment: Accepted by A&A Letters
summary: Low-Ionization Nuclear Emission-line Regions (LINERs) commonly host ionized gas outflows, but their role as high-energy particle accelerators remains debated, particularly following the very-high-energy $γ$-ray detection of NGC 4278, which implied extreme radiative efficiencies. We empirically determine the $γ$-ray radiative efficiency of a local sample of LINERs to test whether their high-energy emission can be powered by extended ionized outflows or requires compact nuclear jets. We combine spatially resolved optical integral-field kinematics from the Multi-Espectrógrafo en GTC de Alta Resolución para Astronomía at the Gran Telescopio de Canarias, yielding ionized-outflow kinetic powers, with 17 years of Fermi-Large Area Telescope observations to derive 0.05--500 GeV luminosities or 95% confidence upper limits. We place the sample in an optical/$γ$-ray diagram alongside archetypal starbursts and radio galaxies. We present the first empirical upper limits on the $γ$-ray radiative efficiency of LINER outflows as a population. No LINER is formally detected ($TS \geq 16$). The strongest constraint is obtained for the radio-loud LINER NGC 1052, with $η< 41%$. For the remaining sources, the Fermi-LAT limits generally lie well above the outflow kinetic powers ($η\gg 100%$), while three sources show marginal hints of emission ($9 < TS < 16$). We conclude that extended ionized outflows in LINERs are highly inefficient high-energy particle accelerators, analogous to starburst superwinds. These constraints disfavor the outflows as the sole origin of extreme $γ$-ray efficiencies and favor compact nuclear jets for the most efficient $γ$-ray-emitting LINERs.

No LINER is formally detected; upper limits show outflows are highly inefficient particle accelerators (η << 41% for NGC 1052, η >> 100% for others), disfavoring outflows as the sole origin of extreme γ-ray emission and favoring compact nuclear jets.
AI.motivation: The debate over whether LINER-hosted ionized outflows can act as high-energy particle accelerators—especially after the very-high-energy γ-ray detection of NGC 4278 implied extreme radiative efficiencies—needs empirical testing. The authors aim to determine whether outflows or compact jets power the high-energy emission in LINERs.

These are combined with 17 years of Fermi-LAT observations to obtain 0.05–500 GeV luminosities or 95% confidence upper limits, and the sample is placed in an optical/γ-ray diagram alongside starbursts and radio galaxies to compute γ-ray radiative efficiencies.
AI.result: No LINER is formally detected (TS ≥ 16). The tightest constraint is for the radio-loud LINER NGC 1052 with η < 41%. For other sources, Fermi-LAT limits lie well above outflow kinetic powers (η >> 100%), while three sources show marginal hints of emission (9 < TS < 16).
AI.conclusion: Extended ionized outflows in LINERs are highly inefficient high-energy particle accelerators, analogous to starburst superwinds. These constraints disfavor outflows as the sole origin of extreme γ-ray efficiencies and favor compact nuclear jets for the most efficient γ-ray-emitting LINERs.

title: The effect of galaxy interactions on star formation rates in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 21 pages, 20 figures; submitted to MNRAS
summary: Observations and theory indicate that galaxy interactions enhance star formation rates (SFRs). However, the degree of enhancement and its dependence on the properties of the interacting galaxies vary across different studies. In this work, we use the COLIBRE simulations of galaxy formation to investigate the effect of interactions on the SFRs of star-forming galaxies at redshift $z\approx0$. The COLIBRE simulations capture the multiphase nature of the interstellar medium and have volumes up to $200^3$ and $400^3$ cMpc$^3$ at m6 (gas and dark-matter particle mass $\sim10^6~\mathrm{M_\odot}$) and m7 ($\sim10^7~\mathrm{M_\odot}$) resolutions, respectively. After constructing samples of interacting galaxies (with mass ratios $>0.1$) and isolated controls, matched in stellar mass, large- and small-scale environment, and redshift, we show that the average specific SFR (sSFR) of interacting galaxies is enhanced by up to a factor of $\approx2$ for separations of $\approx10$ kpc. The enhancement decreases with pair separation but remains significant out to $\approx200$ kpc. The enhancement increases with increasing numerical resolution, is more pronounced in the central regions of galaxies, and decreases with increasing stellar mass at fixed separation. Mergers with higher mass ratios induce stronger sSFR enhancement. We compare our results with observational data from the SDSS, finding good agreement in the dependence of the mean sSFR enhancement on separation, but underpredicting its normalisation by a factor of $\approx2$. Finally, we show that the pre-merger sSFR enhancement of resolved interactions accounts for $\approx2$ per cent of the $z\approx0$ cosmic SFR density.

AI.tldr: This paper uses COLIBRE galaxy formation simulations to analyze how galaxy interactions enhance star formation rates (SFRs) at redshift z≈0. Interacting galaxies show up to ~2x enhanced specific SFR at ~10 kpc separations, with enhancement decreasing with separation but remaining significant out to ~200 kpc. The effect depends on numerical resolution, stellar mass, and merger mass ratio. Results agree with SDSS observations in trend but underpredict normalization by ~2x, and pre-merger interactions contribute only ~2% to the cosmic SFR density.
AI.motivation: Although observations and theory indicate that galaxy interactions enhance star formation rates, the degree of enhancement and its dependence on interacting galaxy properties vary widely across studies. This work aims to provide a systematic, simulation-based quantification of interaction-driven SFR enhancement and its dependencies.
AI.method: The authors use the COLIBRE galaxy formation simulations, which capture the multiphase interstellar medium, with volumes up to 200^3 and 400^3 cMpc^3 at m6 (~10^6 M_sun) and m7 (~10^7 M_sun) resolutions. They construct samples of interacting galaxies (mass ratios >0.1) and isolated controls matched in stellar mass, large- and small-scale environment, and redshift, then compare their specific SFRs as a function of pair separation.
AI.result: Average sSFR of interacting galaxies is enhanced by up to ~2x at ~10 kpc separations, decreasing with separation but remaining significant to ~200 kpc. Enhancement increases with numerical resolution, is stronger in galaxy central regions, decreases with stellar mass, and is stronger for higher-mass-ratio mergers. Comparisons with SDSS show good agreement in separation dependence but underprediction of normalization by ~2x. Pre-merger interactions contribute ~2% to the z≈0 cosmic SFR density.
AI.conclusion: Galaxy interactions modestly enhance star formation in star-forming galaxies at z≈0, with the effect strongest at small separations and in lower-mass systems. The COLIBRE simulations reproduce observed interaction-driven SFR enhancement trends but underestimate the magnitude, and such interactions contribute only a small fraction (~2%) to the cosmic star formation budget at the present epoch.

title: Impact of Neutrino Flavour Conversion on the Diffuse Neutrino Background from Neutrino-dominated Accretion Flows
comment: Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: Neutrino-dominated accretion flows (NDAFs) are believed to form during the fallback accretion phase of some core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe). Such systems produce copious neutrino emission, whose cumulative contribution over cosmic history forms the diffuse NDAF neutrino background (DNNB). As neutrinos propagate from the source to Earth, flavour conversion can significantly modify the observed neutrino spectra and consequently the detectability of the DNNB. In this work, based on fallback CCSN simulations, we investigate the effects of progenitor mass, metallicity, and initial explosion energy on neutrino emission from NDAFs. We calculate the heavy-lepton neutrino ($ν_x$) spectra from NDAFs and incorporate them into DNNB predictions. We find that the unoscillated $ν_x$ spectra are more than an order of magnitude lower than those of electron antineutrinos $\barν_e$. Using the latest neutrino oscillation parameters reported by the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), we evaluate the impact of flavour conversion on the DNNB and derive the corresponding spectra for both the normal and inverted mass orderings. We further estimate the expected event numbers in JUNO and Hyper-Kamiokande. We find that the predicted DNNB signal is strongly dependent on the neutrino mass ordering. While the DNNB may be detectable in the normal ordering with next-generation neutrino detectors, the signal is significantly suppressed in the inverted ordering, making detection considerably more challenging.

AI.tldr: This paper models the diffuse neutrino background from neutrino-dominated accretion flows (NDAFs) formed during fallback accretion in core-collapse supernovae, incorporating flavour conversion with JUNO's latest neutrino oscillation parameters. The authors find that unoscillated heavy-lepton neutrino spectra are over an order of magnitude lower than electron antineutrinos, and that the predicted DNNB signal depends strongly on neutrino mass ordering—potentially detectable in normal ordering but significantly suppressed in inverted ordering at JUNO and Hyper-Kamiokande.
AI.motivation: To understand how flavour conversion modifies the observed neutrino spectra from NDAFs and how this affects the detectability of the diffuse NDAF neutrino background, which has not been systematically characterized before.
AI.method: Based on fallback CCSN simulations, the authors compute heavy-lepton neutrino spectra from NDAFs as a function of progenitor mass, metallicity, and initial explosion energy. They incorporate these into DNNB predictions and apply the latest neutrino oscillation parameters from JUNO to evaluate flavour conversion for both normal and inverted mass orderings, then estimate detection event rates at JUNO and Hyper-Kamiokande.

The predicted DNNB signal is strongly mass-ordering dependent: detectable in the normal ordering with next-generation detectors, but significantly suppressed in the inverted ordering, making detection considerably more challenging.
AI.conclusion: The detectability of the DNNB hinges critically on the neutrino mass ordering; while next-generation detectors like JUNO and Hyper-Kamiokande may detect the signal under normal ordering, the inverted ordering renders it much harder to observe.

title: The Shape of the Vertical Action Distribution Locates the Scatterers that Heat the Galactic Disc
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to the OJAp
summary: The Milky Way's stellar disc is thicker than the cold gas layer from which its stars form. What scatters stars onto orbits with greater vertical motion remains unresolved. Scatterers could fill the disc volume, as bending waves or dark substructure would, or could be confined to the midplane, as giant molecular clouds are. Scattering from a midplane layer occurs only during the fast plane-crossing phase and becomes less effective as that speed increases, whereas a volume-filling perturbation remains effective near the slow turning points. We derive the distribution of vertical action this leaves behind, for any height distribution of scatterers. The geometry turns out to enter only through the logarithmic slope of the diffusivity in action, $D\propto J_z^{b}$, and solving the Fokker-Planck equation gives $p(J_z)\propto\exp[-(J_z/J_0)^{2-b}]$. Scatterers that fill the volume give $b=1$ and an exponential, a thin layer at the midplane gives $b=1/2$ and a sharper cutoff: the shape of $p(J_z)$ records where the scatterers sit, the growth of its scale how strongly they scatter. We fit this model to 7589 low-$α$ red clump stars of Ting & Rix (2019) between 5 and 10 kpc and 2 and 8 Gyr old, leaving the heating history free. This yields $b=0.51^{+0.06}_{-0.07}$, consistent with the thin-layer prediction but not the volume-filling one. Comparing the 2-4 Gyr heating amplitude with the present molecular surface density gives an effective scatterer mass of $2.7\times10^{6}\,M_\odot$. Older stars have experienced more of the Galaxy's gas-richer past; correcting for that history brings all four age bins to $(1.9-2.8)\times10^{6}\,M_\odot$, inside the range cloud catalogues and mass functions give. The Milky Way's disc is heated near the plane, by an evolving population of objects of giant-molecular-cloud mass.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the vertical heating of the Milky Way's stellar disc is caused by midplane-confined scatterers (giant molecular clouds), not volume-filling perturbations. By deriving the distribution of vertical action for any scatller height distribution and solving the resulting Fokker-Planck equation, the authors find the vertical action distribution p(Jz) has a shape diagnostic of scatterer location. Fitting to 7589 red clump stars yields b=0.51, consistent with thin-layer (midplane) scattering, and the inferred effective scatterer mass (~2-3×10^6 M_sun) matches giant molecular cloud catalogs and mass functions.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing question of what causes stars to be scattered onto orbits with greater vertical motion in the Milky Way's disc—whether the scatterers fill the disc volume (e.g., bending waves, dark substructure) or are confined to the midplane (e.g., giant molecular clouds).
AI.method: The authors derive the distribution of vertical action produced by scattering, for any height distribution of scatterers, showing that the geometry enters only through the logarithmic slope b of the diffusivity D∝J_z^b. Solving the Fokker-Planck equation yields p(J_z)∝exp[-(J_z/J_0)^(2-b)]. They fit this model to 7589 low-alpha red clump stars from Ting & Rix (2019) between 5-10 kpc and 2-8 Gyr old, leaving the heating history free, and also correct for the Galaxy's gas-richer past.
AI.result: Fitting yields b=0.51±0.07, consistent with the thin-layer prediction (b=1/2) but excluding the volume-filling prediction (b=1). Comparing the 2-4 Gyr heating amplitude with the present molecular surface density gives an effective scatterer mass of 2.7×10^6 M_sun. Correcting for the gas-richer past brings all four age bins to (1.9-2.8)×10^6 M_sun, within the range given by cloud catalogues and mass functions.
AI.conclusion: The Milky Way's stellar disc is heated near the plane by an evolving population of objects of giant-molecular-cloud mass, demonstrating that the shape of p(J_z) records where the scatterers sit and its scale growth records how strongly they scatter.

title: High-energy neutrino signatures of embedded GRB jets in AGN disks: a dynamic jet-propagation framework
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, and 2 tables
summary: Relativistic jets embedded in active galactic nucleus (AGN) accretion disks are promising high-energy neutrino sources, but their emission is often estimated from a single representative jet state. We develop a time-dependent framework that follows jet-head propagation, evolving reverse-shock conditions, and particle cooling until the jet chokes or breaks out, and apply it to the SG and TQM disk models. For the representative choked cases, neutrino emission is dominated by the high-dissipation phase near jet stalling, allowing a stalling-state approximation to reproduce the trajectory-integrated, detector-weighted event yield within approximately $14\%$. In breakout cases, however, rapid jet-head acceleration across steep disk-density gradients suppresses reverse-shock dissipation and can cause single-state estimates to overpredict the fluence, even after accounting for the available energy budget. Full trajectory integration also reshapes the high-energy spectral tail and produces distinct detectability patterns across SMBH mass and disk radius for the two disk models. Some lower-density outer-disk cases develop harder tails extending into the 10--100 PeV range, motivating future ultra-high-energy neutrino searches. Resolving jet propagation dynamics is therefore indispensable for evaluating embedded transients across AGN disk environments and avoiding systematic biases in multi-messenger modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a time-dependent framework for modeling relativistic jets embedded in AGN accretion disks, tracking jet-head propagation, reverse-shock evolution, and particle cooling. It shows that single-state approximations are reliable for choked jets (within ~14%) but fail for breakout cases due to rapid jet-head acceleration, and that full trajectory integration reveals distinct spectral and detectability patterns across SMBH mass and disk radius.
AI.motivation: Existing estimates of high-energy neutrino emission from relativistic jets in AGN accretion disks often rely on a single representative jet state, which may introduce systematic biases. A time-dependent treatment of jet propagation is needed to accurately evaluate embedded transients.
AI.method: The authors develop a time-dependent framework that follows jet-head propagation, evolving reverse-shock conditions, and particle cooling until the jet either chokes or breaks out. The framework is applied to the SG and TQM disk models, with trajectory-integrated, detector-weighted event yields computed.

For breakout cases, rapid jet-head acceleration across steep density gradients suppresses reverse-shock dissipation, causing single-state estimates to overpredict the fluence. title: Evidence for the First Globular Cluster Stellar Stream beyond the Milky Way
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. This version of the article has been accepted for publication in Nature, after peer review, but does not reflect post-acceptance improvements. The Version of Record is available online at: http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10878-w
summary: The dark matter content of ultra-diffuse galaxies is the subject of considerable debate. Stellar streams, which form when a host galaxy tidally strips stars from an orbiting stellar system, provide a powerful technique to constrain the dark matter content of external galaxies. The stripped stars form long, thin leading and trailing tidal arms that persist for billions of years. Stellar streams from globular clusters are particularly sensitive probes of dark matter halos and substructure. Globular cluster streams are expected to exist in a variety of host galaxy types, but so far, they have only been observed in the Milky Way. We present evidence for the first extragalactic globular cluster stellar stream, identified in deep Hubble Space Telescope imaging of the ultra-diffuse galaxy, UGC9050-Dw1. The stream's morphology, colour, and apparent association with a compact source support the globular cluster progenitor interpretation observationally, and we reproduce the observed surface brightness with simulated globular cluster stellar populations. We use generative stream modelling, which fits dynamical models directly to the stream morphology, to constrain the mass of the progenitor and present the first stream-based halo constraint for an ultra-diffuse galaxy. The stream models point to a globular cluster origin and suggest a massive dark matter host halo. By extending the reach of globular cluster stream analysis to external galaxies, this work opens a new chapter in dark matter science.

AI.motivation: The dark matter content of ultra-diffuse galaxies is debated, and stellar streams provide a powerful probe of dark matter in external galaxies. However, globular cluster streams—particularly sensitive tracers of dark matter halos and substructure—had only been observed in the Milky Way until now.
AI.method: The authors identify the stellar stream in deep Hubble Space Telescope imaging of the ultra-diffuse galaxy UGC9050-Dw1. They validate the globular cluster progenitor interpretation using stream morphology, colour, and association with a compact source, and reproduce the observed surface brightness with simulated globular cluster stellar populations. They employ generative stream modelling to fit dynamical models directly to the stream morphology, constraining the progenitor mass and deriving the first stream-based halo constraint for an ultra-diffuse galaxy.
