AI.conclusion: This work extends globular cluster stream analysis to external galaxies, opening a new avenue for dark matter science by enabling halo constraints in distant systems beyond the Milky Way.

title: A systematic comparison of green valley selection criteria across multiparameter spaces using a homogeneous ultraviolet-optical dataset
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: We present a systematic comparison of commonly adopted green valley (GV) selection criteria by examining their distributions across multiple observational and physical parameter spaces. Using a homogeneous ultraviolet-optical dataset constructed from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we construct GV samples based on rest-frame $u-r$ and NUV$-r$ colours, specific star formation rate, and the $D_n(4000)$ spectral index. These samples are analysed in colour--stellar mass, colour--magnitude, and star formation rate--stellar mass diagrams. We find that the different selection criteria identify statistically distinct subsets of GV galaxies occupying different regions of parameter space. Ultraviolet-based selections are compact in NUV$-r$ colour space but shift toward optically red galaxies and lower star formation activity in the star formation rate--stellar mass plane. The $u-r$-selected sample is more tightly confined in optical colour space but is biased toward higher star formation rates, whereas the $D_n(4000)$-based selection yields the most heterogeneous population. In contrast, the sSFR-selected GV sample exhibits the most consistent behaviour across all parameter spaces. Despite these differences, all selection methods span a similar stellar mass range, indicating that the observed variations arise primarily from differences in star formation activity rather than stellar mass. The relatively small overlap between the different selection criteria demonstrates that GV identification is strongly diagnostic-dependent and that the commonly adopted one-dimensional definitions are not interchangeable. These results highlight the importance of combining complementary diagnostics to obtain a more complete and physically meaningful picture of transitional galaxy populations.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares five commonly adopted green valley (GV) galaxy selection criteria (u-r colour, NUV-r colour, sSFR, and D_n(4000)) using a homogeneous GALEX+SDSS ultraviolet-optical dataset. The different criteria identify statistically distinct subsets of GV galaxies, with each selection biased toward different physical properties, and the selection methods are not interchangeable.
AI.motivation: Green valley galaxies represent a transitional population between star-forming and quiescent galaxies, but the definition of "green valley" varies across the literature depending on the selection diagnostic used. Understanding how these different selection criteria relate to each other and to underlying physical properties is essential for interpreting GV galaxy results from different studies.
AI.method: The authors construct a homogeneous sample from GALEX and SDSS photometry. They define GV galaxies using four distinct criteria: rest-frame u-r colour, NUV-r colour, specific star formation rate (sSFR), and the D_n(4000) spectral index. The resulting samples are then analyzed and compared across multiple observational planes: colour-stellar mass, colour-magnitude, and star formation rate-stellar mass diagrams.
AI.result: The different selection criteria identify statistically distinct subsets of GV galaxies. UV-based selections are compact in NUV-r colour space but biased toward optically red and lower-SFR galaxies. The u-r-selected sample is tightly confined optically but biased toward higher SFRs. The D_n(4000)-based selection yields the most heterogeneous population, while the sSFR-selected sample is the most consistent across parameter spaces. All methods span a similar stellar mass range, so differences stem from star formation activity rather than stellar mass. Overlap between criteria is small, confirming they are not interchangeable.
AI.conclusion: GV identification is strongly diagnostic-dependent, and one-dimensional selection criteria cannot be used interchangeably. Combining complementary diagnostics is necessary to obtain a complete and physically meaningful picture of galaxies in transition between the blue cloud and the red sequence.

title: The Delay Time Distribution of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, accepted to ApJL
summary: Quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) are quasi-periodic X-ray bursts observed in the nucleus of a galaxy. Multiple pieces of observational evidence link QPEs to tidal disruption events (TDEs), which occur when stars are disrupted after approaching a supermassive black hole too closely. Post-starburst galaxies are overrepresented among the host galaxies of both TDEs and QPEs, though the mechanism causing this overrepresentation is unknown. While their physical origin is unclear, the delay time distribution (DTD) of QPEs, or rate of QPEs as a function of time since a burst of star formation, can constrain what mechanisms influence the QPE rate and possible QPE formation channels. We compile a catalog of 10 QPE host galaxies with optical spectra, model the stellar populations with Bagpipes, and retrieve the age of the most recent burst of star formation to construct the DTD of QPEs. We find that the QPE rate increases with post-burst age to reach a peak at ~1 Gyr relative to a control sample, similar to the observational TDE DTD, though we cannot rule out a flat distribution of burst ages relative to a control sample. However, the fraction of QPE host galaxies with high (>1%) burst mass fractions is larger than the fraction of galaxies with high burst mass fractions in either a sample of TDE host galaxies or a sample of control galaxies. If the preferred QPE formation channel requires extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), then such EMRIs may be more readily produced by large, ~1-Gyr-old bursts of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs the delay time distribution (DTD) of quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) by modeling stellar populations in 10 QPE host galaxies, finding that the QPE rate peaks at ~1 Gyr post-burst, with a larger fraction of high burst mass fractions compared to TDE hosts or controls.
AI.motivation: QPEs are linked to tidal disruption events (TDEs), and post-starburst galaxies are overrepresented in both. However, the mechanism causing this overrepresentation is unknown. Constraining the QPE delay time distribution can shed light on the physical formation channels of QPEs (e.g., extreme mass ratio inspirals) and what influences the QPE rate.
AI.method: The authors compile a catalog of 10 QPE host galaxies with optical spectra, model their stellar populations using the Bagpipes code, and retrieve the age of the most recent burst of star formation to construct the DTD of QPEs. They compare this against a control sample and a sample of TDE host galaxies.
AI.result: The QPE rate increases with post-burst age, peaking at ~1 Gyr relative to a control sample, similar to the observational TDE DTD (though a flat distribution cannot be ruled out). Notably, the fraction of QPE host galaxies with high (>1%) burst mass fractions exceeds that in both TDE host and control galaxy samples.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that if QPEs arise via extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), such EMRIs may be more readily produced by large, ~1-Gyr-old bursts of star formation. The similar DTD shape to TDEs supports a shared physical connection, while the distinct burst mass fraction preference hints at a potentially unique formation pathway for QPEs.

title: CHANG-ES XL: Magnetic Field Structures in the Disk and Halo of NGC 891
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present new Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array S-band (2-4 GHz) observations of the edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 891, complemented by C-band data, to investigate the structure of its radio continuum halo. Using rotation measure synthesis we detected an extended polarized halo, with most spatially extended polarized emission confined to Faraday depths within +/- 150 rad m-2. We identified a localized region in the north-east side of the galaxy that shows an enhancement in polarized intensity (not in percentage polarization). By combining the radio data with H-alpha and diffuse X-ray maps, we discuss a possible origin for this structure: a superbubble powered by clustered supernovae. Across the disk and halo, the percentage polarization decreases toward the midplane but shows a mild wavelength dependence, despite the edge-on orientation of NGC 891. This behavior implies that the depolarization cannot be dominated by small-scale Faraday rotation within the disk. Instead, it is possible that most of the observed polarized emission arises on the Earth-facing side of the galaxy. Our peak rotation measure (RM) map shows a smooth transition along the major axis, consistent with a large scale axisymmetric magnetic field. Using H-alpha and UV data, we analyzed the distribution of H II regions and found that they are parts of different spiral arms. We also identified a faint, isolated H II region at a galactocentric radius of 16.9 kpc, with both H-alpha and far-UV counterparts, indicating star formation outside the thin disk.

AI.tldr: New VLA S-band and C-band observations of NGC 891 reveal an extended polarized radio halo with Faraday depths within ±150 rad m⁻². A localized polarized-intensity enhancement in the northeast may be a superbubble from clustered supernovae. Depolarization is not dominated by small-scale Faraday rotation in the disk, suggesting most polarized emission arises from the Earth-facing side. The RM map shows a smooth transition along the major axis, consistent with a large-scale axisymmetric magnetic field. Hα and UV data reveal H II regions distributed in multiple spiral arms, including a faint isolated H II region at 16.9 kpc indicating star formation outside the thin disk.
AI.motivation: To investigate the structure of the radio continuum halo of the edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 891, including its polarized emission, magnetic field structure, and the interplay between star formation, outflows, and the magneto-ionic medium.
AI.method: Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array S-band (2-4 GHz) observations complemented by C-band data, analyzed using rotation measure synthesis. Radio data are combined with H-alpha and diffuse X-ray maps to investigate a localized polarized-intensity enhancement, and with H-alpha and UV data to map H II regions.
AI.result: An extended polarized halo is detected with Faraday depths within ±150 rad m⁻². A localized polarized-intensity enhancement in the northeast is attributed to a superbubble powered by clustered supernovae. Percentage polarization decreases toward the midplane with mild wavelength dependence, implying depolarization is not dominated by small-scale Faraday rotation in the disk; most polarized emission likely arises on the Earth-facing side. The peak RM map shows a smooth transition along the major axis consistent with a large-scale axisymmetric magnetic field. H II regions belong to multiple spiral arms, including a faint isolated H II region at 16.9 kpc with H-alpha and far-UV counterparts, indicating star formation outside the thin disk.
AI.conclusion: The polarized halo of NGC 891 is likely dominated by emission from the near (Earth-facing) side, with a coherent large-scale axisymmetric magnetic field. Localized features such as the northeast superbubble indicate active star-formation-driven outflows shaping the halo, while the detection of an isolated outer H II region suggests star formation occurring beyond the thin disk.

title: From Cluster Cores to the Low-Density Field: Strong Environmental Quenching of Galaxy Star Formation at Low Redshift
summary: We investigate how galaxy star formation activity depends on environment using a sample of 81,647 SDSS galaxies selected over $0.03\leq z\leq0.075$ and $9.7\leq\log_{10}(M_\star/h^{-2}M_\odot)\leq11.0$, including 18,426 members from 572 clusters in the \texttt{GalWCat19} catalog. We characterize environment in two complementary ways: (1) nearest-neighbor density for the full sample, and (2) clustercentric radius and host halo mass for \texttt{GalWCat19}. The sSFR distribution remains bimodal across all environments, with distinct quenched and star-forming components. As local density increases, the quenched component becomes more prominent, while the characteristic sSFR of the star-forming component decreases by approximately $0.29$--$0.35$ dex from the lowest- to highest-density classes. Within clusters, the quenched fraction decreases with increasing projected clustercentric radius, while the star-forming peak shifts by approximately $0.42$ dex toward lower sSFR from the outskirts to the inner cluster region. This extends the picture from previous studies, in which environmental trends are primarily associated with changes in the quenched fraction, by showing that galaxies remaining in the star-forming population also exhibit systematically suppressed sSFR in denser environments. The dependence on host halo mass is weaker and is most apparent among lower-stellar-mass galaxies in the inner cluster regions. By measuring the environmental quenching efficiency at fixed stellar mass, we find excess quenching in cluster environments beyond that expected from stellar-mass quenching alone. These results show that environment is associated not only with an increased probability of quenching, but also with suppressed star formation among galaxies that remain star forming, with local density and clustercentric radius showing the strongest associations.

AI.tldr: Using 81,647 SDSS galaxies (including 18,426 cluster members from 572 GalWCat19 clusters), this study shows that galaxy star formation activity depends on environment not only through an increased quenched fraction but also through systematically suppressed sSFR among galaxies that remain star-forming in denser environments. Local density and clustercentric radius show the strongest associations, while host halo mass has a weaker effect, primarily affecting lower-mass galaxies in cluster cores.
AI.motivation: Previous studies have established that environmental density correlates with galaxy quenching, but it remains unclear whether environment also suppresses star formation in galaxies that remain star-forming, rather than only changing the ratio between quenched and active populations.
AI.method: The authors analyze 81,647 SDSS galaxies at 0.03≤z≤0.075 and 9.7≤log(M*/h^-2 M_sun)≤11.0, including 18,426 cluster members from 572 clusters in GalWCat19. Environment is characterized via (1) nearest-neighbor density for the full sample and (2) clustercentric radius and host halo mass for clusters. The sSFR distributions are examined across environments, and environmental quenching efficiency is measured at fixed stellar mass.
AI.result: (1) The sSFR distribution remains bimodal in all environments. (2) As local density increases, the quenched fraction increases and the star-forming peak shifts ~0.29–0.35 dex lower in sSFR. (3) Within clusters, quenched fraction decreases with clustercentric radius while the star-forming peak shifts ~0.42 dex lower toward cluster centers. (4) Host halo mass dependence is weaker, most apparent for lower-stellar-mass galaxies in inner regions. (5) Excess environmental quenching persists beyond stellar-mass quenching alone.
AI.conclusion: Environment is associated both with an increased probability of quenching and with suppressed star formation among galaxies that remain star-forming, with local density and clustercentric radius being the strongest environmental drivers.
